title: Presenting results
goal: Give a short formal presentation in Indonesian: open it properly, move from part to part with the right signposts, present numbers precisely, handle questions, and close it the way an Indonesian audience expects.
bekal: structure a talk: *Pada kesempatan ini…, pertama-tama, selanjutnya, sebagai penutup*
present data: *meningkat dari tiga juta menjadi lima koma delapan juta*
handle questions: *Terima kasih atas pertanyaannya; kalau saya tidak salah tangkap…*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Gladi bersih
dialogs.intro: A Thursday in mid-November, two days before the Sumberwangi village festival, in the project office at the balai desa. Sarah will present the project's results on the main stage, with the Bupati in the front row. Dr. Lestari has agreed to play the audience.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Silakan mulai, Mbak Sarah. Anggap saja saya Pak Bupati.
lines.id: Go ahead, Sarah. Imagine I'm the Bupati.
lines.literal: please start, Miss Sarah. consider just I Mr Bupati.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Baik. Selamat pagi, Bapak-Ibu sekalian. Hari ini saya mau cerita soal hasil proyek kita.
lines.id: Right. Good morning, everyone. Today I want to tell you about how our project went.
lines.literal: good. safe morning, Sirs-Madams all. day this I want tell matter result project our.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Berhenti sebentar. “Mau cerita soal” terlalu santai untuk acara resmi.
lines.id: Stop there a moment. “Want to tell you about” is too casual for a formal event.
lines.literal: stop a-moment. “want tell matter” too relaxed for event official.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Jadi sebaiknya bagaimana, Bu?
lines.id: So how should I put it?
lines.literal: so best-its how, Mrs?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: “Pada kesempatan ini, izinkan saya memaparkan hasil proyek desa wisata Sumberwangi.”
lines.id: “On this occasion, allow me to present the results of the Sumberwangi tourist village project.”
lines.literal: “at opportunity this, permit I expound result project village tourism Sumberwangi.”

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Memaparkan. Baik, saya catat. Lalu pertama-tama saya jelaskan latar belakangnya.
lines.id: *Memaparkan.* Right, I'll note that. Then, first of all, I explain the background.
lines.literal: expound. good, I note. then first-first I explain background-its.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Bagus. Setelah itu data. Berapa jumlah kunjungan sejak April?
lines.id: Good. After that, the data. How many visits since April?
lines.literal: good. after that data. how-many number visit since April?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sekitar dua ribu wisatawan. Pendapatan homestay naik hampir dua kali lipat.
lines.id: About two thousand tourists. Homestay income has almost doubled.
lines.literal: around two thousand tourist. income homestay rise almost two time fold.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Jangan hanya “hampir dua kali lipat”. Sebutkan angkanya: dari berapa menjadi berapa.
lines.id: Don't just say “almost doubled”. Give the figures: from what to what.
lines.literal: don't only “almost two time fold”. mention number-the: from how-much become how-much.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Rata-rata pendapatan per homestay meningkat dari tiga juta menjadi lima koma delapan juta rupiah per bulan.
lines.id: Average income per homestay rose from three million to five point eight million rupiah a month.
lines.literal: average income per homestay rise from three million become five comma eight million rupiah per month.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Nah, itu meyakinkan. Selanjutnya, tantangan dan rencana ke depan. Jangan hanya yang indah-indah.
lines.id: Now that's convincing. Next, the challenges and plans for the future. Not just the pretty things.
lines.literal: there, that convincing. next, challenge and plan to front. don't only which beautiful-beautiful.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Termasuk soal banjir dan sampah plastik?
lines.id: Including the flood and the plastic rubbish?
lines.literal: including matter flood and rubbish plastic?

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Justru itu. Pendengar lebih percaya pada pembicara yang jujur tentang masalahnya.
lines.id: Exactly. An audience trusts a speaker who is honest about the problems.
lines.literal: precisely that. listener more trust in speaker who honest about problem-its.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Baik. Sebagai penutup, saya ucapkan terima kasih atas perhatiannya.
lines.id: Right. And to close: thank you for your attention.
lines.literal: good. as closing, I say thank you for attention-its.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Sempurna. Tapi siapkan juga jawaban kalau Pak Harun bertanya soal dana tahun depan.
lines.id: Perfect. But have an answer ready in case Pak Harun asks about next year's funding.
lines.literal: perfect. but prepare also answer if Mr Harun ask matter fund year front.

notes: **Anggap saja…** — “just pretend, consider that…”. *Anggap saja rumah sendiri* (make yourself at home, literally “consider it your own house”) is what every Indonesian host says to a guest.

**Bapak-Ibu sekalian** — “ladies and gentlemen, everyone”. *Sekalian* after a group means “all of you”. It is the neutral way to address an audience, and it works in a village hall, a university and a ministry alike.

**Mau cerita soal → memaparkan.** Dr. Lestari's correction is about register, not grammar. *Cerita soal* is what you do with friends; *memaparkan* (to set out, to present, from *papar*, flat and open) is what you do on a stage. Its noun, *paparan*, is the formal word for a presentation.

**Izinkan saya…** — “allow me to…”. It is the polite way to announce your own actions in a formal setting: *izinkan saya memperkenalkan diri*, *izinkan saya menjawab*. Compare *mohon izin* from Unit 13.

**Lima koma delapan.** ⚠️ Indonesian uses a comma for decimals and a full stop for thousands: *5,8 juta* is 5.8 million, and *2.000* is two thousand. Say the comma aloud: *lima koma delapan*. Getting this wrong on a slide is a classic foreigner's mistake.

**Justru itu** — “that's exactly it, precisely because of that”. Dr. Lestari uses *justru* to turn Sarah's worry into the reason to do it. You have now met *justru* as “on the contrary”, “that's just the problem” and “precisely”: it always marks something that runs against expectation.

grammars.title: Signposts for a formal talk
body: An Indonesian audience expects to hear the structure of a talk out loud. These phrases are the skeleton; fill in the flesh between them.

head: Job
Indonesian
English
rows: On this occasion, allow me to present…
This presentation is in three parts.
To close, … / That concludes my presentation.

after: *Demikian* (thus, so) marks the end of almost anything formal: a speech, a letter, a report. *Demikian yang dapat saya sampaikan* — “that is what I am able to convey” — is the humble version, and very common.
The last line is fixed: *Terima kasih atas perhatiannya* (thank you for your attention), often followed by a religious closing greeting in the same form as the opening one.

grammars.title: Presenting numbers
body: Numbers in a talk come with a small set of verbs and prepositions. *Dari … menjadi …* (from … to …) is the most useful frame of all.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: as many as two thousand tourists
on average, more than, almost, about

after: *Sebanyak* before a number is typical of reports and news (Unit 11): it adds weight without adding meaning. In conversation, just say the number.
*Meningkat* and *menurun* are the formal pair; *naik* and *turun* work everywhere. Use the formal pair on slides and in written reports.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Tanya jawab di panggung
dialogs.intro: The festival, Saturday morning. Sarah has given her presentation to a hall full of villagers, students and officials, with the Bupati in the front row. Pak Harun, as moderator, opens the floor.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Demikian paparan dari Mbak Sarah. Kami buka sesi tanya jawab. Silakan, Bapak-Ibu.
lines.id: That was Sarah's presentation. We now open the question-and-answer session. Please, ladies and gentlemen.
lines.literal: thus presentation from Miss Sarah. we open session ask answer. please, Sirs-Madams.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Terima kasih. Saya Ratna, dari kelompok homestay. Apakah program ini tetap berjalan setelah Mbak Sarah pindah?
lines.id: Thank you. I'm Ratna, from the homestay group. Will the programme carry on after Sarah moves away?
lines.literal: thank you. I Ratna, from group homestay. whether programme this remain run after Miss Sarah move?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih atas pertanyaannya, Bu Ratna. Jawabannya: ya. Mulai bulan depan, pengelolaannya diserahkan kepada Pokdarwis Sumberwangi.
lines.id: Thank you for the question. The answer is yes. From next month, management passes to the Sumberwangi tourism group.
lines.literal: thank you for question-the, Mrs Ratna. answer-its: yes. start month front, management-its is-handed-over to Pokdarwis Sumberwangi.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Kalau boleh saya tambahkan, UGM juga tetap mendampingi selama dua tahun.
lines.id: If I may add, UGM will also continue to support us for two years.
lines.literal: if may I add, UGM also remain accompany during two year.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Betul, Pak. Pertanyaan berikutnya, silakan. Ya, Mas yang di belakang.
lines.id: That's right. Next question, please. Yes, you at the back.
lines.literal: correct, Sir. question next, please. yes, Mas who at back.

lines.speaker: Yoga:
lines.text: Yoga, dari UGM. Pertanyaan saya agak nakal, Mbak: apa yang paling susah selama proyek ini?
lines.id: Yoga, from UGM. My question's a bit cheeky: what was the hardest thing about this project?
lines.literal: Yoga, from UGM. question my rather naughty, Miss: what which most difficult during project this?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Pertanyaan yang bagus. Jujur saja, yang paling susah adalah belajar kapan harus diam dan mendengarkan.
lines.id: Good question. Honestly, the hardest thing was learning when to be quiet and listen.
lines.literal: question which good. honest just, which most difficult is learn when must silent and listen.

lines.speaker: Ratna:
lines.text: Sama belajar bahasa Jawa, Mbak!
lines.id: And learning Javanese!
lines.literal: with learn language Javanese, Miss!

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Itu juga, Bu. Nuwun sewu kalau bahasa Jawa saya masih belepotan.
lines.id: That too. Forgive me if my Javanese is still all over the place.
lines.literal: that also, Mrs. [nuwun sewu] if language Javanese my still messy.

lines.speaker: Harun:
lines.text: Mboten napa-napa, Mbak. Sumberwangi sekarang juga rumah panjenengan.
lines.id: It doesn't matter at all. Sumberwangi is your home now too.
lines.literal: not what-what, Miss. Sumberwangi now also house you.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Matur nuwun, Pak. Terima kasih, Sumberwangi, atas perhatian dan kebersamaannya.
lines.id: Thank you so much. Thank you, Sumberwangi, for your attention and for having me as one of you.
lines.literal: thank you, Sir. thank you, Sumberwangi, for attention and togetherness-its.

notes: **Kami buka sesi tanya jawab.** The moderator (*moderator*) uses *kami* because he speaks for the organisers, not the audience. *Tanya jawab* (ask-answer) is the Q&A; on a programme it is often shortened to *diskusi*.

**Saya Ratna, dari…** At a formal event, a questioner first gives name and affiliation, thanks the speaker, and only then asks. Even Bu Ratna, who has worked beside Sarah for months, follows the ritual on stage. Skipping it sounds abrupt.

**Pokdarwis** is the *Kelompok Sadar Wisata*, “tourism-aware group”: the village community body that runs a *desa wisata* in Indonesia. Handing the project to them is exactly what a good community-tourism project is supposed to do.
**Kalau boleh saya tambahkan** — “if I may add”. The polite way to join in on somebody else's answer. Its partner is *Mohon izin menanggapi* (may I respond), used when you want to disagree.

**Pertanyaan yang bagus. Jujur saja…** Praising the question buys you a second to think, in Indonesian as in English. *Jujur saja* (to be honest) signals that a real answer is coming, not a diplomatic one; the audience relaxes when they hear it.

**Nuwun sewu, mboten napa-napa, panjenengan, matur nuwun.** Javanese *krama*, the polite register. *Nuwun sewu* is “excuse me, forgive me” (Unit 13), *mboten napa-napa* is *tidak apa-apa*, *panjenengan* is a respectful “you”, and *matur nuwun* is “thank you”. Pak Harun switches into Javanese at the end because what he says is personal, not official.

grammars.title: Handling questions
body: Q&A has its own formulas, for the moderator and for the speaker. Knowing them lets you concentrate on the answer instead of the frame.

head: Phrase
English
Who says it
rows: We now open the floor to questions.
Please, the gentleman on the left.
*Kalau saya tidak salah tangkap, Ibu menanyakan…*
If I've understood correctly, you're asking…
I'll send you those figures later.
We're short of time: one more question.

after: *Kalau saya tidak salah tangkap* (if I haven't caught it wrongly) is the most useful phrase here for a foreigner. It lets you check you have understood a long question, and nobody minds.
⚠️ If you do not know the answer, say so: *Mohon maaf, untuk hal itu saya belum bisa menjawab sekarang.* An honest “not yet” is respected; an invented answer is remembered.

sections.title: The shape of an Indonesian presentation

blocks.text: A formal presentation in Indonesia is framed by greetings and thanks at both ends. It can feel long to a foreign speaker, but leaving the frame out feels rude to the audience, like starting a letter without “Dear…”.

head: Part
What goes in
Typical words
rows: *Selamat pagi, salam sejahtera bagi kita semua.*
acknowledging the important guests, by rank
gratitude for the chance to speak
*Demikian paparan saya. Mohon maaf apabila ada kekurangan.*

blocks.text: *Mohon maaf apabila ada kekurangan* (forgive any shortcomings) is not false modesty; it is expected, and it closes almost every formal talk. B2 will take the opening greetings further, including the religious ones.

Both mean “we”, and a presenter has to choose all the time. *Kita* includes the audience; *kami* leaves them out. Choosing well makes the villagers owners of the project; choosing badly makes them spectators.

blocks.title: Slide headings
items: Slide headings are noun phrases with capitals on each main word; slide bullets need no full stops.
